reason: The CONFLICT claim does not hold up under an enforcement-reality check. I fetched both cited sources: prompt-audit.md confirms "an audit that finds nothing should change nothing... an empty diff beats a manufactured one," with re-audit triggered by model migrations, no fixed cadence, and nothing about a minimum-deletion count or an anti-regrowth mechanism; code.claude.com/docs/en/memory.md confirms /doctor's CLAUDE.md trim check and /doctor prompt-audit are purely advisory and on-demand ("nothing in your files changes until you ask Claude to apply them"), with only a vague "periodically" for review cadence, no gate, and the trim check scoped to the checked-in CLAUDE.md, not the rule files. The house rule's own text already says exactly this ("The harness proposes trims when asked and advises periodic review, but sets no cadence and lets a trimmed file grow back"), so it is accurately describing, not misrepresenting, the native feature. The alleged internal self-contradiction is a misreading of scope: "delete at least one section across the root file and the rule files each time" is an aggregate expectation over the whole fixed-cadence pass across all docs, while "finding no candidate is valid" is the per-file release valve; the rule's own Anchor line confirms only the ratchet (non-regrowth) is mechanically gated by `npm run check:house`, not a hard per-file deletion count, which matches this repo's stated "judgment over hard rules" posture rather than contradicting the native audit's "empty diff is fine" philosophy — the two actually agree. Critically, the house rule supplies a real mechanical gate (the ratchet that tightens on every shrink and blocks a trimmed file from growing back) plus an independent fixed cadence spanning the root file and every rule file collectively, neither of which the purely advisory, on-demand, manually-applied native /doctor features provide at all.

The cited page (prompt-audit.md) verbatim contains both quotes the claim leans on: "An audit that finds nothing should change nothing - a clean surface is a valid outcome, and an empty diff beats a manufactured one," and, in its verify step, "Re-audit at every model release. Prompts are per-model artifacts... Each new migration section in shared/model-migration.md is the trigger to run this audit again." The companion doc named in the evidence (code.claude.com/docs/en/memory.md) confirms the two native features are real and scoped as asserted: "/doctor prompt-audit" runs this exact file ("The audit runs through the bundled /claude-api skill"), and a separate "/doctor" CLAUDE.md trim check is documented nearby ("The /doctor checkup proposes trims for a checked-in CLAUDE.md... The trim check requires Claude Code v2.1.206 or later"). I also re-read the house rule's own prose directly ("Trim on a fixed cadence, delete at least one section across the root file and the rule files each time... finding no candidate is valid, since the prompt to look is what does the work"), and it does carry the literal tension the claim describes: an imperative to delete something on every pass sits beside a clause validating finding nothing, unlike the native audit's clean, single-track "empty diff is fine" stance. Since the citation says exactly what the claim attributes to it, at the scope asserted (the prompt-audit procedure, not the unrelated trim-check specifics), and the paraphrase of the house rule text checks out against the rule file itself, the claim survives this documentation-accuracy check.

Fetching both citations confirms the content overlap the claim describes for two of the three sentences (the "skip plan mode when the diff fits one sentence" advice and the "clear after two failed corrections" fix are both on the best-practices page in near-identical wording and strength), but the disposition still fails on enforcement/delivery reality, not category: the best-practices page is written to the human operator ("run /clear," "ask Claude to create a plan") and is never loaded into a Claude Code session's context, whereas this rule lives in `.claude/rules/house/claude-code.md`, which this repo's own CLAUDE.md names as the loaded source of truth for every session here, i.e. an instruction actually delivered to the model each time, not a webpage a person may or may not have read. "Anchor: none" only concedes there is no automated check for compliance, not that the guidance fails to reach the session the way the harness's docs page does. The third sentence -- "re-read the source of a ruling immediately before you act on it, not once at session start" -- is also not actually stated by either citation: the prompt-caching page only explains the mechanical fact that an edited root/user CLAUDE.md doesn't apply mid-session until /clear, /compact, or a restart (and separately notes path-scoped rules load later and take effect once read), it never advises proactively re-reading a ruling's source before acting, and it says nothing about non-CLAUDE.md sources of a ruling (an issue thread, a PR review comment, a skill file) at all. Given the delivery-mechanism gap on the first two sentences plus the outright novel content of the third, DUPLICATE overstates the case.

reason: The claim's own evidence undercuts its CONFLICT verdict: native subagent/teammate/workflow model resolution falls back to the session model unless CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL is set, and the house rule's actual text directs adopters to do exactly that (".claude/rules/house/claude-code.md", "Set the model explicitly on every subagent and workflow agent": "set the subagent model variable in user settings to the tier below the session's as the floor; an explicit call-level model still wins") — so the rule is invoking the native mechanism the claim cites, not contradicting it. More importantly, the rule's real enforcement does not stop at that env var, which is exactly the part the claim flags as non-portable across adopters' machines: the repo ships five roster agents under plugins/house/agents/*.md (scout=haiku, researcher/builder=sonnet, refuter/debugger=opus) with model, effort, and tools mechanically pinned in YAML frontmatter that the harness reads and enforces regardless of whether CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL is set anywhere, plus a SessionStart hook (plugins/house/hooks/session-start.mjs) that automatically injects the "Model tier" directive text (plugins/house/orchestration/ORCHESTRATION.md, "A subagent, teammate, or workflow agent runs below the session by default") into every session's context on startup/clear/compact, no configuration required on the adopter's part. The repo's own receipts confirm this was a deliberate design response to precisely the gap the claim raises: "the variable is a floor, not a way of working, and the way of working was being retyped into prompts... The plugin now ships it" (docs/handbook/claude-code.md, lines ~226-248). So the native feature is the lever this rule pulls (a documented, working mechanism), and the house layer adds mechanically-enforced roster pins plus automatic session-start delivery that the bare native resolution order does not give a fresh adopter on its own. That is enforcement and portability the harness's opt-in env var lacks by itself, not a conflict with it.

reason: Fetched both cited pages directly. code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents states the opposite of the claim's evidence: "By default, a subagent can spawn subagents of its own, up to three layers below the main conversation," and the Agent tool is withheld only "at the depth limit" (or when explicitly omitted via tools/disallowedTools), not by default in general; the built-in general-purpose subagent's tool list explicitly includes Agent. So "Agent tool withheld from subagents by default" and "the built-in agents cannot spawn" are factually wrong readings of the citation. The real native mechanism is a configurable spawn-depth limit (CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH, default 3, set to 1 to disable nesting) plus a per-agent tools/disallowedTools omission -- both of which house's roster (ORCHESTRATION.md) actively exercises ("Each pins its model, effort, and tools, and none can spawn an agent") rather than inheriting for free. The house bullet is therefore not restating behavior already enforced on a main session that "cannot change it"; the main session's own roster config is precisely what overrides the harness's more permissive default.

If the file is near a limit, Claude Code reminds Claude to shorten it... If the file is over a limit, the write still succeeds, but Claude Code returns an error...'. But the claim overreads this into a contradiction that isn't there. The same docs section opens with the load-time fact the rule's header (the comment above checkLengths in plugins/house/payload/check.mjs, lines 1438-1441) restates almost verbatim: 'The first 200 lines of MEMORY.md, or the first 25KB, whichever comes first, are loaded at the start of every conversation. Content beyond that threshold is not loaded at session start' -- with no notice described at that load event itself. The write-time reminder/error is a separate mechanism that fires only when Claude writes to the file that session, not a notice given when an already-oversized file is silently loaded and truncated. The house rule's own comment already cites the write-time floor by name one paragraph above the 'no notice' line ('Native floor: the harness already measures its own auto-memory index when Claude writes it and warns or errors there, so this family's memory warning is a second surface... never the primary limit'), so it is not ignorant of or contradicting the documented write-time behavior; it is building on it. This matches the harness research bank's own verified classification for this exact item: ~/Documents/house-rules-harness-research/2026-09-20/classifications/main-classify-mechanisms.json lists 'lengths family' as disposition COMPLEMENT, action 'keep', with evidence stating 'the file already declares that native floor in its own comment' -- not CONFLICT. The claim's own evidence text even undercuts its stated CONFLICT disposition by conceding 'the rule-file length limits themselves complement the native warnings.' The citation supports COMPLEMENT, not CONFLICT, so the claim fails at the scope asserted.

reason: The claim's evidence mischaracterizes the harness default. Per this repo's own survey of https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents (docs/handbook/sources/harness-survey.md), a subagent is NOT stripped of the Agent tool by default: "a subagent can spawn subagents of its own, up to three layers below the main conversation" (default depth 3, tunable via CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH), and the harness "withholds the Agent tool from every subagent except a fork" only once that depth limit is reached — the survey's own "Default subagent tool filter" row says Agent is removed "(at depth limit)," not unconditionally. The built-in general-purpose subagent explicitly "has every subagent tool," so by default it retains Agent and can nest; only the read-only Explore/Plan built-ins, and the five pinned house-rules roster agents (scout/researcher/builder/refuter/debugger, whose `tools:` allowlists in plugins/house/agents/*.md omit Agent), are actually blocked from spawning. The house rule's bullet ("Subagents do not spawn subagents. They report back." — plugins/house/orchestration/ORCHESTRATION.md:51) is injected only into the orchestrating session's own context by a SessionStart hook scoped to `startup|clear|compact` (plugins/house/hooks/hooks.json), a different event from the SubagentStart/SubagentStop lifecycle subagents get — so it is a directive to that session's judgment when it spawns ad hoc or off-roster subagents (e.g. the general-purpose agent), not a restatement of something the harness already withholds from them. Without this rule, an off-roster or general-purpose subagent the session spawns would keep the Agent tool and could nest up to the harness's default depth of 3; the "main session that cannot change it" framing is backwards, since the orchestrating session controls exactly that by what tools it grants a spawned agent. The rule therefore tightens the harness's looser, per-agent depth-limit/tool-filter mechanism into a stricter, session-wide zero-nesting policy the harness does not itself provide. That is scope and posture the native mechanism lacks, so DUPLICATE does not hold.

reason: The CONFLICT claim conflates two distinct, non-contradictory harness moments. Live docs confirm: (1) "The first 200 lines of MEMORY.md, or the first 25KB, whichever comes first, are loaded at the start of every conversation. Content beyond that threshold is not loaded at session start" with no notice given at that load-time moment, and separately (2) "After Claude writes to MEMORY.md, Claude Code measures the file against the 200-line and 25KB read limits" and reminds/errors only then. The house rule's "no notice" language (in the checker's header comment and ADR 0008) refers specifically to the silent load-time cut, not to writes, so it is not contradicted by the write-time reminder/error the claim cites -- both are true simultaneously, since they fire on different triggers (session load vs. Claude's own write). Enforcement reality also defeats the conflict even setting that apart: the write-time reminder is an ephemeral in-session nudge invisible to CI, reviewers, or a later audit, and it never fires for a file that is already over-limit for reasons other than Claude's own write (a hand edit, a different machine, a stale copy); the house `lengths` family instead leaves a persistent, CI-visible warning (never a finding, per ADR 0008, precisely because the state is machine-local and unfixable by PR) that catches exactly that gap. Separately, the native "instruction-file length warning" the claim also cites is a startup/`/status` warning only -- never blocking, no ratchet, no required written justification to exceed -- while the house `lengths` family mechanically blocks (exit 1) a configured ceiling on the root file, rule files, README, and skill bodies via `npm run check:house`/CI, with a ratchet that only tightens and a deviation-ledger requirement to raise it. None of that exists natively. This matches the rule text's own framing ("The harness already shortens the index after a write and errors past the load ceiling; treat that as the floor and add what it cannot see") and the survey's own pre-existing, skeptic-reviewed classification of "lengths family" as COMPLEMENT (not CONFLICT), action reword-to-cite-native-floor.
